utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon everybody. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor verse Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, all the accused are present. Prosecution, I see we have some added elements to your team. Mr. McCloskey, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Yes, we have a new lawyer, Jelena Plamenac, who is helping us out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shorten the time of translations, I suppose. Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic for the Beara team, Mr. Krgovic for the Gvero Defence team, and that's it. As you would have noticed, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today, Judge Kwon couldn't be with us, and so we are proceeding accordingly. Mr. Milosevic, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Had you cooperated straight away with the Tribunal when we issued this subpoena, we would have had this sitting last week and all lawyers here would have had less trouble. You avoided contempt proceedings just like that. I hope there will not be a repetition of this if you are summoned as a witness later on in any other trial, and I expect you to apologise to the Trial Chamber for having behaved the way you did. Before we proceed any further, since you are a witness here, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration prior to testifying to the effect that you will be testifying the truth and the whole truth. The text of the solemn declaration has already been handed to you, please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, a warning, a caution? Yes, I was going to come to that, but I wanted to ask Mr. Bourgon first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I wanted to say exactly this, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Witness, you lived through parts of the events that we are talking about, and there is a possibility that questions may be put to you which, if answered truthfully by you, could expose you to criminal proceedings. I am not saying that this will be the case, but I cannot exclude the possibility, and because of that, by law I am bound to caution you and explain to you the rights that are available. First of all, under our Rules, Rule 90 in particular, if questions are put to you which, if answered truthfully, could expose you to criminal proceedings you have a right to ask the Trial Chamber to exempt you from answering such questions. This is not an absolute right. We may accede to your request and exempt you from answering such questions, in which case that would be the end of the story as far as those questions are concerned, or we can force you to answer those questions. If we force you to answer those questions, you are bound to answer them truthfully, but you have a further right then and that is that whatever you say in the reply to such incriminatory questions cannot be made use of against you in any criminal proceedings or in any proceedings that might be taken, unless these proceedings are for perjury, for false testimony. Have you understood what I have explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can, therefore, now proceed. Mr. Bourgon or Ms. Nikolic, I don't know, but I saw Mr. Bourgon ready to stand up. Mr. Bourgon, how long do you expect your examination-in-chief to last.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. I did indicate to the parties in the courtroom, but I failed to inform the Trial Chamber, I expect to take about an hour and a half and no more than two hours to finish the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Haynes, you had given some indication that you might have got involved in this witness as well. Do you intend to put questions to him on cross-examination or do you wish to reserve your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think everybody knows my position because I sent them all an e-mail this morning, which is at this very, very, late stage of proceedings, I take the view that this witness has come to deal with a very narrow and discreet issue that arose from the evidence of the witness summoned by the Trial Chamber to give evidence. And that has absolutely no interest to me or my client at all, and on that basis, I do not propose to cross-examine him, but I would hope that the parameters of his evidence are kept within sensible bounds given the very late stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. And you, Mr. McCloskey, of course you haven't heard the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hope I would -- wouldn't take no longer than the Defence would take on direct and hopefully less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's try and finish this witness today, and we need to finish before quarter to 7.00, not 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon Judges, good afternoon colleagues in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Mr. Milosevic. Can you hear me, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I see you are looking at the screen in front of you. I am not sure if you can see -- if you can see me on the screen before you or you can look at me. It's as you wish. So allow me first to begin, sir, to begin -- for the record to introduce myself. My name is Stephane Bourgon. We have had the pleasure of meeting this week, and today I am accompanied with members of the Nikolic Defence team. Ms. Jelena Nikolic and Mrs. -- sorry, Ms. Chloe Grandon, and together we represent Drago Nikolic in these proceedings. I have quite a number of questions for you today, but I will try to make this as short as possible. What is very important is that if at any time you do not understand a question that I may ask you, do not hesitate to stop me and to ask me to clarify this question. Do you understand this, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. To begin with, please state your full name and date of birth for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Sreten Milosevic, I was born on the 17th of February, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how old are you today, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Going straight to the events, in July 1995 I believe you were a member of the VRS. Which unit were you a member of at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Zvornik Brigade in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what was your rank then, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall when exactly you joined the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In September of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. So would I be correct that by July 1995 you had been in the Zvornik Brigade for about ten months; is that more or less the case?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That being the case, can you tell us how well you knew the members of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the ten months I was there and in view of the fact that the brigade had more than 4.000 military conscripts, I can say that I got to know the narrow group of people who were in command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where were you born, Mr. Milosevic, and where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Lupoglava, Kladanj municipality. I attended the primary school in Stupari, Kladanj municipality. I completed the secondary school in Banovici, and I obtained my degree in Brcko whereupon I worked in the mine near Zivinice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name of the mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the name of the mine again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Djurdjevik mine in Djurdjevik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, by July 1995, how familiar were you with the various location in the area of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I was not familiar that well with the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what position you held in the Zvornik Brigade from the time you joined until July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I arrived in the brigade in September of 1994, I became deputy or advisor to the assistant commander for logistics. Several months later, I was appointed assistant commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is that assistant commander of the complete brigade or assistant commander of the logistics?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was your immediate superior in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The brigade commander was, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if the commander was absent, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the commander's absence, it was the Chief of Staff who was in charge of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall who that was in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall who were the other assistant commanders of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Assistant for moral guidance and religious matters and assistant for security of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember who held those positions in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Assistant commander for moral guidance was Mr. Simic, and assistant commander for security was Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall who was responsible within the Zvornik Brigade for intelligence matters?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The responsible individuals for intelligence were Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what was your working relationship with Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was no professional relationship since I was in charge of logistical support. We did not have any dealings, so we did not get into contact with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are there any occasions when you met in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We would meet during the briefings by Mr. Pandurevic which normally took place in the morning and did not take place that often, that would we would meet there occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how often, if at all, did you socialise with Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not that often. As I said, it was periodical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in your capacity as assistant commander for logistics, can you describe, in a few words, what exactly was your job within the Zvornik Brigade? What did you deal with?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The duties of logistical support, or, rather, my duties were to provide supplies for the life and work of the brigade; in other words, food provisions, clothing, fuel, and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about transport? Did that come under you as assistant commander for logistics?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Under the establishment of the logics support there existed a logistics battalion which had in its possession certain vehicles and was manned with mechanics who did their duties both in respect of transport vehicle -- vehicles and combat vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this battalion, sir, what was the relationship, if any, between that battalion and yourself?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I had a relationship with the Chief of Staff of the logistics battalion, and on occasion, I would contact the battalion directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me make my question a bit more precise: Were you in command of the logistics battalion?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in July of 1995 and throughout the period of time you spent with the Zvornik Brigade, did you perform the function of brigade operations duty officer?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the duty officer of the brigade in extraordinary situations. There was this one period when there was an extraordinary situation, but I asked the commander, Mr. Pandurevic, to relieve me of this particular duty so that I am no longer a part of the group of duty officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, who was the brigade operations duty officer on 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was that, to your recollection, a normal duty?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall other times when you were or when you performed the function of brigade operations duty officer?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It also happened that there would be occasional extraordinary duty stints, since the Zvornik Brigade was deployed in other AORs for the purposes of the VRS. Therefore, even those who were not permanent members of duty -- of the group of duty operations officers would sometimes perform that duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you perform the function of operations duty officer at the IKM or forward command post of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall any dates when you were operations duty officer at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I could not recall the dates, but you showed them to me in your office when it was that I was on duty at the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you recognise your signature on those -- on the dates that I showed you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I go back to the period of service for the brigade operations duty officer, how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Normally, 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was that always the case?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes the duty stint might exceed the 24 hours to 26 or even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, to your recollection how often did the brigade operations duty officer, whether at the brigade or at the IKM, perform a double shift or a two-day shift?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It did not happen often, but I am aware of certain instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at what time did the operations duty officer in the brigade begin his period of duty?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One would start a new period of duty between 7.00 and 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was that always the case or were there exceptions to this, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was the rule, but it would so happen that the time would shift because it was impossible to keep to the exact times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, as the brigade operations duty officer, were you assisted by anyone?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Normally there would be the chief duty officer and his assistant who would be appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And tell us a bit about the duties of the assistant, when was he on and when was he off?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The duty officer would start his duty from the hand-over time for the subsequent 24 hours. Now, the assistant duty officer would have his stint from 12.00 a.m. -- or, rather, 12.00 p.m. until 5.00 the subsequent morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that would be -- am I correct in saying that this would be during the night?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 12.00 midnight until 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where was, sir, the office of the brigade operations duty officer located?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The office of the operations duty officer was upstairs in the building of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall in which room it was?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As one ascends the stairs on to the first floor, the office is immediately to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, at this time I would like to show you an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in e-court please 3D110.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, this exhibit will appear on the screen before you. And my first question is: I would like to know if you are familiar with this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would like to have page 2, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you familiar, sir, with this floor plan?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the layout of rooms on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask you now to make some markings on this floor plan. I will ask the Court Usher to give you a special pen. I believe this must have been explained to you, and I will ask you to make some markings on this exhibit. And first, I would like you to indicate by a 1, with a circle around it, in the duty officer room.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall where your office was, and if so, to indicate this with a 2 with a circle.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you recall where the commander's office was, that is Commander Pandurevic as you identified him, can you put a 3.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the office of Dragan Obrenovic with a 4, if you know where that is.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall where the office of Drago Nikolic was at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, looking at this floor plan, are you able to tell which side of the building had a view on the road? And if so, if you can put a 6 with a circle around it on the side which gives a view to the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He just forgot to say 5 is Drago Nikolic's office, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I did not say it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, sir, can you confirm that the 5 with a circle around it is the office where Drago Nikolic was?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the 6 -- is that where the side of the road with this building?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the Zvornik-Bijeljina region road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you indicate with a 7, with a circle around it, where the Drina River would be compared to this building.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can just ask you, sir, to, on the bottom right corner, simply to put your initials and the date, which is 15 July 2009.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would like to save this exhibit for admission purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did you share your office with anyone at the time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I shared my office with Mr. Mijatovic. He would be very often present in that office with me, Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I won't be needing the Court Usher anymore. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall who was on duty, if anyone, at the entrance of the brigade command building on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think there was a duty officer on the ground floor in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall if there was a person on duty on the first floor of the command building in the hallway where your office was and the other offices were?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, there had never been any duty officer stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the last time that you saw the brigade operations duty officer notebook?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I saw it in your office when you showed it to me. That was the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall, having looking at that book -- or were you able to say who was the duty officer the day before you on 12 July?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also showed me the handwriting, but I did not recall who the duty officer was before my duty stint. You told me it was Mr. Maric, I still don't remember that, and I am not familiar with his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recall or were you able to tell who was the brigade operations duty officer on the 14th of July, the day after you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, Mr. Dragan Jokic took up the duty after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what was, if you remember, the rank and position of Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what position did he hold at the time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Chief of the engineering service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, given, sir, that you did mention that you did look at the brigade operations duty officer notebook, what was your impression when you look at the entries for the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The entries for the 13th of July could easily be seen there. I -- my handwriting is normally very poor, and I made notes on that day during my shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, going back to that period of time - and I'm talking of the day that you are on duty - what information did you receive on that day concerning the 28th Division, or you might have referred to it as the column of soldiers; what information did you have on that day?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Part of the entries I made when I was operations duty officer included a note to the effect that the columns of the 28th Division were sent through the Zvornik area toward Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how important was this information to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was important at the time in view of the fact that Commander Pandurevic was not present in the brigade and that some of the brigade units went away together with Mr. Pandurevic. In other words, the brigade was not at full strength, and there was a threat to the brigade if the column of the 28th Division was to pass through the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall what actions or whether any actions were taken in that respect concerning the column?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is an entry in the book which says that the commander, or, rather, his deputy, Mr. Obrenovic, issued an order to raise the level of combat readiness of certain units and that the personnel who were outside resting be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, is this something that you can tell the Trial Chamber just from reading the book, or is this something that you remember?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is what I read in the notebook while I was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, what information, if any, did you have or did you receive on 13 July 1995 concerning prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, when I was on duty, I didn't receive any information or any -- or any knowledge about any prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, during this same evening of 13th July, what information, if any, did you obtain concerning members of the brigade being ordered to provide security for prisoners at any location?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I had no information whatsoever, and one can see that from the operations duty officer notebook that there was no entry concerning this particular issue, because had it been the case, the duty of the duty operations officer would be to record it in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, on the evening of 13 July what information, if any, did you receive concerning events or any event taking place at the Orahovac school?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive any information on the evening of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, that evening of 30 July -- 13 July, I apologise, do you recall leaving the brigade operations duty officer room at any time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I left my post that night at 2400 hours, and I went to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And before that, do you recall leaving the room at any time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I may have gone to the toilet or to have breakfast or lunch or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, was there any rule concerning the brigade operations duty officer concerning where he was supposed to stay during his period of service?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The operations duty officer must be in his office during his shift. That was not a rule, that was his duty, an obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, when you say "his office," is that his own office or the operations duty officer office?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the day when he's on duty, he should stay in the operations duty officers' room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, today as we sit here, do you know someone by the name of Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall when you first met that person?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My first encounter with Mr. Momir Nikolic was sometime in 1997 on the premises of the company called Stamparija [phoen] where he was the manager, and that was the first time that I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell us a bit more about the context of your encounter with Mr. Momir Nikolic at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1996, when I left the VRS in the month of May, I started my own business. I was involved in the sales of consumer goods, and by looking for business opportunity, I ran into a friend who wanted to introduce me to this printing plant and allow me to establish some business contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall if any information was exchanged between you and Momir Nikolic during this encounter?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When we met first, he told me that he was a security -- he used to be a security officer with the Zvornik Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, where was this business that you visited when this encounter took place?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We met in an office inside this company or this printing plant, and I still don't know where it is located, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But the shop itself, do you recall where the shop itself is? In which town is the shop? This printing shop.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall what was the relationship between this printing shop and Momir Nikolic, what was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I came there, he worked as the manager of this printing shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recall seeing this person, Momir Nikolic, when you were brigade operations duty officer on 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I already said that I saw him for the first time in 1997, which means that I had never met him in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall, going back to the evening of 13 July, 1995, if any officer who was not a member of the Zvornik Brigade visited Standard Barracks that evening?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember anyone from some other brigade paying a visit. And in order for them to visit the brigade at any given time, an entry to that effect would be made in the book of the operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on that evening of 13 July 1995, did anyone come to you introducing themselves as the chief of security of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is this something you would remember, and if so why?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I already said that any visits from other brigades or strangers coming to the brigade would require the procedure to be applied by them going through the gate and then the officer there in charge would bring such individuals to the operations duty officer, and then it was -- would be up to him to decide whether to accommodate the person who wants to visit the brigade or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on that evening of 13 July, 1995, did anyone come to you, if you recall, asking to see Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know where Drago Nikolic was on the evening of 13 July?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know where Drago Nikolic was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know who the military police on duty at the gate were during the evening of 13 July?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I know that there was an officer on duty, but I don't remember because I didn't know the names of people who were in the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how do you know if there was somebody there that night?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whatever situation occurs, and particularly if there is an emergency, two military policemen had to be on duty at the gate in order to monitor the entry and exit of both individuals and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, if -- do you recall, sorry, if any military policemen on duty at the gate contacted you during the evening of 13 July?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. But, as I said before, according to the rules, if I would -- if I should receive a call from the gate, then I would have recorded that in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall who decided who -- which officer would be on duty, whether at the brigade or at the forward command post, at any given time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think that that was the task of the Chief of Staff and the operations sector of his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, during the evening of 13 July, while you were the brigade operations duty officer, do you recall if there was a change of duty officer at the forward command post that evening?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, do you know who is Mihajlo Galic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galic worked for the personnel service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember his rank?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What contact did you have, if any, with Mihajlo Galic on 13 July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I had no contact with Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You said earlier that you went to bed at midnight. At what time did you wake up and resume your functions as duty officer?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I continued my duty as operations duty officer at 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you replace -- sorry, can you tell us what you did that morning?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That morning I handed over my duty because of -- I first recorded what I did and then on the 14th, I handed over the duty to the next officer who was supposed to take it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you have any contact that morning with Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Once you had been replaced as brigade operations duty officer, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I went to my office to do my everyday job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, what do you know or what can you tell us about buses with prisoners driving in front of Standard Barracks on that day?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that on that day I either received information or heard somebody commenting about convoys of buses passing from Srebrenica via Zvornik to Bijeljina. Given that my office was opposite of the road, I had to get out of my office in order to see this convoy of vehicles that was travelling from Zvornik to Bijeljina and after that, I went back to my office and resumed my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions which are -- which come from your answer. First you said "convoys," with an S. Were the people speaking about one convoy or many convoys of prisoners driving in front of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have information that there were a number of convoys. I did see a convoy on that occasion when I went out, but I don't know how many of them were in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you count the buses, and who, to the best of your knowledge, was inside these buses?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not count the buses. According to what you saw, those were Muslims onboard the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, until you saw those buses on that day, what information did you have about the presence of prisoners in the area of Zvornik up to that point?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that particular moment, I didn't know anything about prisoners in Zvornik. At that moment, I realised that buses were passing by with Muslims onboard, but I didn't know that they were prisoners. How could I have known that? I only knew that they were being transported from Zvornik in the direction of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, this brings one more question from me concerning the population of Srebrenica, the women, the children, and the elderly; do you know what happened to them in about the same time-frame?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you aware at that time that the Zvornik Brigade had sent buses to Bratunac with respect to the transport of the population there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of any buses from Zvornik Brigade going there and even if we had buses at the time, for that matter, I just simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, later that day - now I bring you back to the time that you saw those buses -- let me take that over again. What time was it when you saw those buses driving in front of Standard Barracks?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact hour, it might have been during the morning, 10.00, 11.00, I can't tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, are you aware that any of these buses stopped or would have stopped at the Standard Barracks that day?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I don't remember them stopping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you ever hear any rumors about buses that would have stopped at Standard Barracks on that day?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, do you recall having an interview with the Prosecution where you discussed the buses that you saw passing in front of Standard Barracks?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall what time you said that you saw the buses in front of Standard Barracks?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember telling them at what time they were passing by the Standard Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, later that day did anything happen to you in relation to the people or the -- that were carried in these buses?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, i.e., the 14th of July, somebody - I don't remember who it was - came to my office and said that Chief Obrenovic had ordered that everyone should go to Orahovac to guard the prisoners. So that was the time when I learned about prisoners being held in Orahovac. We provided security in order to prevent escalation on the ground because that was a populated area that needed to be secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you remember who told you to go to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I already said that I don't remember even the face of the person who came to my office and passed on this order to go to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you help us in identifying where this order came from?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I already said that the order came from Chief Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall exactly what these words were that were mentioned by the person who told you to go to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Chief Obrenovic ordered that everybody, with the exception of the operations duty officer, should go to provide security in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier where was your office on the first floor of the command building and where was the office of the operations duty officer. Is it possible that the person who told you to go to Orahovac was the duty officer Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know where Dragan Obrenovic was that day?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know where he was exactly. All I know was -- all I know is that he was in the zone of responsibility of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you go to Orahovac on that day, and if so, who went with you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Orahovac on that day; however, I don't remember who went with me to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you did get to Orahovac. How did you travel to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I left my office in front of the gates of the barracks, I entered a luxurious passenger car, I don't remember which make it was, and I was driven to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall anybody else who was in that car with you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some persons with me. I don't remember how many, possibly two, and I also don't remember who they were, who accompanied me to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon when you went to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you the person responsible for the group of persons who went to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what time you left Standard Barracks to go to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon. Now, I can't remember when exactly, but I think it was between 2.00 and 5.00 when I left the barracks and went to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, as you arrived in Orahovac - and I know this might be difficult for you - but can you describe the scene as you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival at Orahovac, I realised that the situation was horrendous, and then I realised that I had been duped. And this happened in this way, I alighted from the vehicle, and I had the school in my view, or, rather, the school-yard, and I saw a vehicle where the Muslims who were blindfolded were being loaded upon, and after that they were driven from Zvornik towards the wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you hear any shooting?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whether it was the second batch of people there who were being loaded, at that point I heard shots being fired in front of the vehicle while the loading was going on. It seems that somebody was shooting at people who were trying to run away; whether there were two or three of them, I couldn't see very good. I did see one of them falling down, one of these Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me make my question more precise: Did you hear shooting coming from the area towards which that vehicle left with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was already 5.00 or 6.00 or 7.00, there were only intermittent shots being heard in the area where these people had been taken to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you exactly, if I --

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was on the road next to the school building and the yard in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what can you say about the prisoners? What did you see of the prisoners? How many, where, how? Describe what you could see and what you knew at the time.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to know what their condition was, because they were kept prisoner in the school gym. I saw the vehicle which was parked by the school, and I saw the ones who were being loaded on to the buses, blindfolded, and with their hands tied. This is what I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you figure out what was happening, sir, at the time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I got out of the car and saw them being loaded on to the buses with blindfolds, I realised that I had been tricked; and I was trying to devise a way for me to go back to the brigade so as not to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So how long did you stay there and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise time; an hour or two. We were invited for a cup of coffee to a house next to the building where I tried to get hold of a vehicle which would take me to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A while later, I don't know exactly how long after, somebody said that a vehicle arrived in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I got out of the house or into the vehicle which had several passenger seats, I remember clearly seeing a child, a tearful child, seated in the vehicle. We went in the direction of Zvornik, and some 300 or 400 metres later, Soldier Tanic emerged on the road, beckoned to us to stop, and we gave him a lift to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this soldier, the name you use is Tanic. Who is he?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tanic was an individual who worked in the financial section of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in Orahovac, did you recognise any of the soldiers present?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, being from the Zvornik Brigade, do you know if these soldiers were from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I already said that I didn't know the conscripts of the Zvornik Brigade. I could only recognise them as members of the VRS but could not tell if they were members of the Zvornik Brigade or any other brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you notice anything special on the uniform of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall observing anything special.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you see any of the soldiers wearing white belts?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, how familiar were you with the members of the military police company of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I already said that I didn't know anybody by name, and I might recall them by their faces and tell who belonged to the Zvornik Brigade if I saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when you arrive in Orahovac, was anyone waiting for you, given that you were told to go there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that anybody was expecting me. When I arrived, there was nobody there waiting for me to give me any instructions. Simply, I found myself outside of the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were wearing any rank insignia?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not wear any rank insignia in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing anyone there wearing a red beret?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing anyone with a red beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you see or meet the person who was responsible for directing the activities there at the school?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I didn't come across anyone who would have been responsible for something like that in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you speak to anyone there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to those who were present there. There were several individuals whom I found when I got there and whom I talked to, but I don't recall if they were civilians or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, talking about civilians, how many did you see and where were they?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were several individuals where I stood. I can't tell you exactly how many; a group of five to six, I believe. I can't tell you how many were soldiers and how many civilians among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, I know that it's difficult, but did you try to intervene while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was not able to intervene. I was not allowed to. Firstly, I didn't know anyone; secondly, had I tried to intervene, I could have ended up faced with the same problem. I was simply trying to think of a way to get out of the situation and be away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, had the loading of the prisoners begun when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As soon as I got out of the vehicle, I realised that prisoners were being loaded on to buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mention "buses," were they loaded on buses or something else?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say they were buses. There was a vehicle with a tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mention earlier that you saw a prisoner or maybe you used two or three, I believe, being shot. How long did that take place after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it happened with the first vehicle which was being loaded, I think it happened when they were getting on to the second vehicle. When exactly, how long after, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, who did you call to get a vehicle to pick you up?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I got into a house by the road and I called the operations duty officer to fetch a vehicle which would take me to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know who was on duty that afternoon or that evening at the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Dragan Jokic on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you speak to Mr. Jokic himself?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember if I talked to him. I know that I placed a call asking for a vehicle to pick me up. I don't recall if I spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how long did it take before that vehicle arrived?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we had a cup of coffee. It may have taken an hour for the vehicle to arrive in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And tell us what you were told when the vehicle arrived.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We were told that a vehicle had arrived outside the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you describe this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that when I got out of the house I saw the vehicle parked by the road in front of the house facing Zvornik. When I got into the vehicle, I observed that it had several seats, but I don't recall the make of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, is this the same vehicle in which you travelled to Orahovac earlier that day?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I had arrived to Orahovac from Zvornik in a limousine, a passenger car; whereas on my way back it was not a luxury passenger car. It was a car with multiple passenger seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, had you seen this vehicle before on that day in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see a single vehicle in Orahovac on my arrival there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And throughout the time that you spent there, did you see that specific or that particular vehicle present there at any time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall who was in the vehicle; for example, can you identify the driver?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that I remembered the child who was crying in the vehicle, and another thing that stuck in my memory was Mr. Tadic [as interpreted] emerging on the road beckoning to us to stop and give him a lift to Zvornik. These are the things I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, the transcript says "Tadic," is it the right name?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tanic. Yes, it says -- it's translated as "Tadic," and it should be "Tanic."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you go straight to Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what time was it when you are arrived at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the evening hours, as it was getting dark, I didn't pay attention to the time, but around the time when darkness started setting in at that time of year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that time of the year, in 1995, about what time was it getting dark?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think that in our region it's between 10.00 and 11.00. That could be the reference point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived at the brigade? Describe what you did.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The vehicle we were on did not get into the brigade compound. It stopped outside of it, and we got out, and I told the driver to take the child to the outpatients clinic or rather to the hospital in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And why did the tell the driver to go to hospital with the child?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, primarily in view of the fact that it was a child and a civilian, it was the most natural thing for the child to be taken to the town hospital of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what did you, yourself, did -- what did you do, sorry, at Standard Barracks?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I got into the barracks, I don't recall exactly if it was already 10.00 or 11.00 by that time, I was getting ready for bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you have dinner that night?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall if I had dinner that night at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you meet with any other people in your office that night?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was no get-together that meaning, I don't recall talking to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall being asked a question by the Prosecution whether there was some kind of a celebration that night?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do, and I told the Prosecution that such a question was absurd, that anything of the sort would cross anyone's mind, that the circumstance would call for any sort of celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, going back quickly to Orahovac, did you see Drago Nikolic there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see Drago Nikolic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know if Drago Nikolic was there in Orahovac on that day?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I heard from those who were present there that Drago Nikolic had been there during the day, but I did not learn the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you ever hear any rumors of Drago Nikolic being at the place where prisoners were being killed?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not hear such rumors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on that day, did you order or make any arrangements for food and drinks to be delivered at Orahovac at any time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall giving any such order, and the brigade documents clearly show if any orders had been issued to make arrangements for food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, just to make sure, I have the feeling you are concluding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the questions I have, I need about 10 to 15 minutes. So we can stop now for a break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- or I can continue for another ten, because we have only been at 100 -- one hour and 20 minutes so far, according to what I'm told. As you wish, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you think you will finish in ten minutes' time then I suggest you can continue and finish and then we will have a break to be followed by cross-examination later. Okay. It seems to be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I might not be able to finish in 10. Fifteen, yes; but ten, no. So maybe it's better if we take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, your last answer concerning the food or drinks, I would like to know if when you were there in Orahovac whether you saw any food or drinks being delivered to anyone?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, given that you were the person responsible for food, as you said, did Standard Barracks have the possibility to produce fresh pastries or did it have fruit juices which could be delivered to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any such possibilities, either for pastries or anything else in terms of specific food stuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, could someone get some fresh fruit juices from the Vitinka bottling company for example, and take that to Orahovac on behalf of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Receiving any sort of assistance or requests for food or anything else in the Zvornik area, all of it had to go through the brigade. Since there had been abuse of procedure before, we asked that it strictly be done through the brigade in order for the food to be distributed. As for juices, nobody ever engaged in distributing juices in the brigade for the brigade's units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So could it be done that day that someone went to Vitinka to get juices on behalf of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of it. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on that day, did you know if prisoners were taken to any other location in the area of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I told you that I learned that they were there when I got to Orahovac, but I was not aware of any other possible locations where they have been -- where they might have been taken in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you find out such information later?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What did you hear later?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Again, I can't recall how many days later this was, but I heard that there were other prisoners from Srebrenica in various other locations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you ever -- did you ever learn who was responsible for the killing of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And much later did you ever hear any rumors about any agency of the VRS who was responsible for the killing of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were rumours in Zvornik that it had been done by the security from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember who said this or who mentioned these rumours?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was off the record. Nobody officially informed anyone of anything, nor did I personally make any inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you have any information based on what you saw and what you did in July 1995 from which you could tell that there was any truth in these rumors?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't make any inquiries. The truth is that what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on a different topic, as assistant commander for logistics, did you have new camouflage uniform and boots in stock?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Within the brigade, we had a warehouse where uniform and boots were stored. We never had a change of new uniforms. We had the old JNA and M77 uniforms. We had old boots which had already been mended, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, could anyone in 1995 promise to give someone a new uniform if they did a certain job?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of it. Promises could have been made, but where uniforms would be got from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on a different topic, are you -- do you recall whether the Zvornik Brigade ever used codes to communicate with its battalions by military field phone?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of it. I am an economist by profession, and I am not familiar with these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who is Vojo Jekic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've heard of Vojo Jekic, but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know who is Ratko Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I know Ratko Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in Standard Barracks?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He would come to see the commander in the barracks from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall if that was the case in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall him visiting in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, the next day on 15 July, do you recall where you were that morning, that's the day after Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was probably in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, that day having a phone conversation with your commander?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't remember it at the time, but from -- I saw it in the operations duty officers' notebook. Again, I point out that I am not familiar with the AOR of the Zvornik Brigade. It was Mr. Mijatovic who was called upon to explain what the situation was in the general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, just a few more questions and we're done. Do you remember meeting - -

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I think the record is probably wrong on the pronunciation of those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Which names are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mijatovic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I heard it say Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, it says Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you say, sir, on that day Mr. Mijatovic spoke to the commander?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and here in my interpretation it says "Mijatovic." Now it says Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall meeting me in Zvornik at any time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall ever meeting with other members of the Nikolic Defence team in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember who you met?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I met Ms. Jelena and Ms. Nevenka

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you ever sign a statement at the request of the members of the Nikolic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you always respond to the questions which were put to you by the members of the Nikolic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Why not? How did you feel when you were contacted by members of the Nikolic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the issue, I am reluctant to deal with anyone. I had already given a statement to the Prosecution, and I had given my statement before the court in Sarajevo. I felt that there was no need for me to give any further statements on the issue to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when you provided answers to members of the Nikolic Defence team, did anyone try to influence you in any way?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did members of the Nikolic Defence team tell you that Momir Nikolic testified in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's -- this could go on, and that's a leading question. He could go on and tell him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's conclude here, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have three questions, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- I think it's important for him to answer this, Mr. President, to simply to say whether we told him that Nikolic -- Momir Nikolic had testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please answer the question and let's conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what were you told exactly concerning Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was told that Mr. Nikolic had visited the Zvornik Brigade on the evening of the 13th and that he asked for someone to take him to the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what was your reaction when you were told this information by the Nikolic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I repeated what I said here. I said that I met Mr. Momir Nikolic for the first time in Bratunac in the company he was working for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, one last question I would like to ask you is simply: Looking back at those events of July of 1995, how do you feel today about those events?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do not feel comfortable at all. It is very hard for me, and I have to say that I am very sorry for everything that happened, especially for the victims. And I'm very sorry that it happened in the AOR of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And maybe one last question I forgot: Why did you refuse to come here when you received the first subpoena?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The summons said that I should come and appear before the Court of my free will, and I refused to do so since, as I already said, I had given my statement to The Hague investigators. That was the reason why I did not respond to the first summons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And further to what the Presiding Judge told you at the beginning, is there anything that you want to say in this regard?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the break, and it will be a strict 20 minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make sure, does any of the other Defence teams wish to cross-examine this witness? Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I am going to reserve my position on that. Things went rather beyond the evidence of Momir Nikolic during the examination-in-chief, but at the moment, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey. Sorry, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't cross-examine the witness also, but unless such a need does arise from the cross-examination of the Prosecution. In that case, I would ask the permission of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you can all ask, of course, but you know what we had decided time back that Defence teams go first on cross-examination followed by the Prosecution. So that has to be bourne in mind. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I -- do you remember us talking in that interview back in January of 2006, you and I?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So on 14 July you, as assistant commander for logistics of the Zvornik Brigade, were at the Orahovac school. Was there any officer superior to you there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said it then and I am saying it now, again, I didn't come across anyone at that particular location who had a higher rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So as assistant commander, you were the highest-ranking, most authoritative person there when that process was going on?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about that, whether my rank was the highest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I know is that I was there at that time, and during that time I didn't see anyone with a higher rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So as far as you knew, you were the one that was responsible and the most responsible military position with the duties incumbent upon you under the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any responsibility or duty at that location, except for an order that I received from the barracks to come and provide security. I considered myself at that point in time to be a physical entity providing security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't feel you had any responsibility whatsoever to do anything to protect any of those Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry that this happened, but I had no capability of doing anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you issue any orders?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you seek out the commander in charge?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say you went and had coffee for an hour, two hours, until dark. Sir --

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said I went to have coffee in the house that was situated opposite the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: While this was going on, you went to have coffee to let all this dirty work be done by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I had be invited for coffee to that house. I don't remember having one, and I didn't allow, nor was I in charge of anything that was going on in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was going on when you got there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the car to Orahovac, I got out of the car on the road in front of the school, and I stood by the fence. I saw prisoners being loaded into a vehicle with their eyes covered with blindfold.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what did you think was going to happen to them?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It crossed my mind that they were going to be shot dead, and that is what actually happened, and then I realised that I had been deceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did it cross your mind that these people were going to be shot dead?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you load people, blindfolded people, and when you drive them into the woods, from the school into the woods, I couldn't imagine anything else happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You knew before you got there that they were going to be executed, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that, because if I had known that, I wouldn't have come to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Maybe we will come back to Orahovac. In the interview that we had in January of 2006, I asked you on page 7 after you had mentioned you were chief of logistics, or assistant commander, excuse me, for logistics, and I said: "And who did you have directly under you?" And you said: "We had chiefs of services, chief of procurement, chief of warehouse, chief of traffic service, and chief of technical service." Then I ask you to name those people. And the first person you name was a Mr. Krstic. What was his job?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krstic was chief of the technical service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then you said the chief of the warehouse was a guy named Bosko. What was Bosko's last name?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
