utterances.text: Bosko Nikolic, was in charge of quartermaster. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who is the chief of traffic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Chief of the traffic service was Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at the time you told me, "I cannot remember the chief of traffic." So why do you remember now?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when I was giving you these answers, I couldn't remember. Now, after some time elapsed, I made some statements in the meantime, and you also refreshed my memory, and so I remembered that his name was Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've heard in this case that Mr. Pantic from Standard sent, on the 15th of July, three cases of ammunition, 7.62, to the Rocevic school that were taken to the execution site at Kozluk. Mr. Pantic was under your direction, surely you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to P04600, I won't spend too much time on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You can take a look at this document on the screen, and you'll see that it's dated 17 July 1995. We've got this from the Zvornik Brigade. The name of the sender was Vezionica, what's Vezionica?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Vezionica was a building next to the barracks. It was a sewing and embroidery plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and we can see from this document that this is the -- camouflage uniforms were supplied, 19 uniforms were for special purposes. So it looks like we had 19 nice new uniforms coming into the Zvornik Brigade on 17 July, and your name is on the bottom of it. So do you want to think back and maybe change your testimony a little bit on that new uniforms business?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, this does look familiar to me. I don't remember this particular sheet at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the signature. I'll give you the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you blow that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd just like if my colleague could tell us, because I can't see with the document I have, where it says "new uniform" in this document. I don't see the word "new" anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was my question. Maybe this fabric place cranks out old uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The witness had already provided information about uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're -- stop, stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If he wants to make a suggestion he should suggest new uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, please. When I intervene, we intervene very, very, little, but when we do, please stick to the rules. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, take your glasses out and take a look at the stamp on the original. Our translation people have put S. Milosevic as what they see there. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have anything that you want to say about this?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember this document at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So these uniforms could have gone to Drago Nikolic and you wouldn't have -- probably wouldn't remember that either; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't see from this document where these uniforms were meant to be going. This deals with the receipt of the uniforms by the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or, rather, there is not even a signature of the person who was the recipient except for the box 42 where we have the signature of the man who entered this document into books, into the register.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is about 19 new uniforms, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Camouflage uniforms," and mark, and then there is a remark about the purpose, but why the person in charge did not sign the receipt of these uniforms. You can see my signature, you can see the signature of the man who entered this in the register, but also missing is the signature by someone from the professional service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What professional service would that be?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's mentioned here Mr. Nikolic, but there is no signature attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let be clear. You're talking about 2nd Lieutenant B. Nikolic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's Bosko Nikolic, the fellah you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another document, P04538.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just will indulge you for a moment to see if you can help me with an issue that came up with another witness, and it's about, I'm sure everyone remembers, forms from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could just show you, and I will give you the photocopies of the forms. If you could just take a look at this -- at this document, and it's making a reference to forms. And I'll try to give you the original -- actually, I'm not sure we need to worry about the original. Here is P00354. Is that one of the forms noted in this particular report? This is a document that makes reference to two specific forms. Is that one form I gave you one of the forms that it's referred to? Obviously not the telegrams, I am not talking about telegrams. I am talking about the attendance roster or the record of the engagement.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is the form that's referred to in the short July 6th note referring to the big form that I gave you that's in your hands? Not that form in particular, but is it the same form?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is the form you have in front of you now the forms that were typically used at the time by the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in each unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that form either an attendance roster or a record of engagement form, that's in front of you right now?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what it says, the engagement record of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's all -- that's all I was asking about. Now, you can give that back to me so it's not -- or give that back to us so it's not a distraction. You may remember when we were talking a while back during your interview I asked you on page 12: "When did you start equipping the unit to be able to move to Srebrenica?" And you said: "I don't remember that there was a concrete equipping, that I was equipping unit by unit." And then I ask you again on page 13: "Do you have any knowledge at all of the preparations of men and materiels to go down to Srebrenica from Zvornik?" And you said: "No, I don't." And having thought about that question, do you want to change your answer today? Let me ask it to you again: What equipment were you involved in helping get the troops ready that went down to Srebrenica in early July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean departure for Srebrenica? Because the translation I received was the departure of men from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I meant for Srebrenica. Do you wish to change what you told me, or do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I stand by my previous answer because I said there was no particular equipping of units because there was no specific task given to the logistics service in terms of what should be specifically provided for anyone for this mission. There might be record of that, somebody might look into it, but I personally don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'll remind you that you didn't tell me back in 2006 that you didn't remember, you said that there wasn't any. And so let's look at a document, you'll see it up on the screen. It's dated 2 July, Military Post 7469, Zvornik, request to the Drina Corps command, and let me give you a copy so you can see the whole thing because it's not on the screen, and the screen, you won't be able to read it if we get any smaller. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In the record, page 49, line 17, the interpreter said there was no specific task given to the logistics service, and the record doesn't reflect that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said before, and I'm telling you again, I don't remember this document. Now I see it and I have been questioned about the events and the equipping of units for Srebrenica. I honestly didn't know the date. I did sign this request, but I could not remember it then, nor would I have been able to remember it now had you not shown it to me. I don't know any specific or special activities being pursued in the brigade at the time. This might have been for the needs of the units that was being equipped prior to going to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you can read it like we all can. It says for the forthcoming operations, and we know when they went down. Do you really want to suggest this is all a question of memory, sir? At the time when I asked you this question you couldn't remember that you gave blankets and mess kits and stretchers to the troops that were going down to a major battle-front. Why don't you just cut to the chase and tell us you lied to me at the time, make it easy.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't lie at the time. It's not true that I knew that and that I didn't want to say that, because there is no reason for that. I really would like to ask this question whether we actually received all these items that had been requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is that your signature at the bottom of this?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I think you're in the best position to answer that question. All right. Let's go to another document. I want to go with you now to the duty officer notebook that you've talked about a bit, it's P00377. And I'll give you the book so you can actually see the original, and it's meant to start at ERN last four digits 5738. For the record, it's -- to help with the English. But if you can open it up, sir, to that -- what's been marked in page 120 in English. There should be a red sticker. I think you're looking at it. And it starts out with breakfast for 80 military conscripts, and please take a moment to study it.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it says, "Breakfast for 8 [as interpreted] military conscripts. Major Obrenovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this note, under that, "Kaldrmica Kasaba several thousand going towards Tuzla," and it says "to Cerska." That's circled. Is that what you were telling Mr. Bourgon about, that you had received information that there were several thousand Muslims going towards Tuzla and towards Cerska the morning of 13 July?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This has been entered in the book on the 13th to the effect that several thousand were moving towards Tuzla. This is the record of the information that we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's your handwriting? You wrote that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did you receive that information from?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember who the information came from because there is no record of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Drina Corps duty officer, perhaps? Bratunac Brigade duty officer, ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is all the handwriting on that page yours?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, it isn't. This portion written in Cyrillic, that's not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And which portion is written in Cyrillic, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Vera [phoen] from Bijeljina called, Rada called, then lieutenant-colonel ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So we are talking right at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the next page. If we go over to the next page, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before we move to the next page, my colleague mentioned, and that is on the transcript, page 51, and that was lines 17 to 20, and I need to bring it back. He said: "Is that what you were telling Mr. Bourgon, that you received information that there were several thousand Muslims going towards Tuzla and towards Cerska ..." That witness never said that to me, so at least if my colleague is going to ask a question, if he wants to quote my question, he should quote my question and the answers of the witness, but not to say something that the witness never mentioned. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you wish to comment, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's how I remembered it. The witness agreed with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move. The witness has heard the exchange anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing controversial about it that I can think of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've made your point. That's what is being put to the witness and who is perfectly capable of agreeing with you if he so wishes, and move on. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go to the next page in the book, and that's ERN, last four digits, 5739, and it's 121 in the B/C/S and English for the computer. And, sir, I'm not so interested in the substance of this writing. I am not going to ask you about anything about what's said, but can you tell me: Is this all your handwriting on this page?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So who do you think stood in for you and wrote in Cyrillic between these two sections of your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember who that might have been, but I know it wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you can't tell how long you were out of the post from this either, can you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page, 122. It's ERN 5740. And again, sir, if you could -- is that all your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you read that part for us, we see it in English, it says "bulldozer," what's it say besides "bulldozer"?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we are not on the same page, which page is that? I can't find that word on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you help him, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's sitting right there in the middle of the page. Just take your time. I know you're -- it says -- sorry, it says "dozer" in B/C/S and got translated as "bulldozer" in English.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did write it but this word, "dozer" doesn't ring any bells. I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, what is a dozer?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what dozer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Isn't a dozer a bulldozer, an earth moving machine? You're a logistics guy, you've got to know what a dozer is.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not quite clear on that, if dozer and bulldozer are one and the same thing, terminology wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's Birac Holding?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's the aluminium plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they have dozers?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Glinica plant, the huge aluminium processing plant. Every time I've driven by there there's been more equipment around. Come on, you've got to remember the heavy equipment at that place.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what these various machines are called. I am not a civil engineer. I am not a civil engineer. I have a degree in economics. I don't know the various terms for machinery still today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember that phone number, 584-700? Do you remember Ziko?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see the entry with the number and the name Ziko, but neither the telephone number nor the name mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's it say after Ziko, if you can make it out? You wrote it.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says "- auto machine."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you wrote the word "dozer," that's your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's now go briefly to Exhibit P04614. This is a -- it's in Cyrillic, and I don't have a translation at the moment. Let me -- it's a two-page document, so it will be easier to give you one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Pardon the handwriting, the handwriting, sir, that's on this is just our English translation, and perhaps we can put that on the -- well, it's simple enough. Can you go to the second page -- well, the first page says: "Telephone book of the 1st Infantry Zvornik Brigade command and units." And we go down the page, on the first page it says: "Important numbers in the VRS," then it goes, "Extensions," and the next page in the B/C/S, "Companies and institutions." And in the second column we see under the phone number 584-700 "Birac Holding." So does that help you at all, sir? You've written down "dozer" and the phone number for Birac Holding and the name Ziko. I'm sure you had contacts at Birac Holding.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I repeat, neither the number nor the name of the person ring any bells. If you ask me a day later, perhaps I'd know as it is. I don't know anything about it, nor did I ever contact Ziko for any sort of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If your commander got you on the line and said, Captain, I need an excavator to improve a trench and a break in the line. Jokic tells me all his are in use. Get me an excavator now. And Pandurevic says that to you. What do you do?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he didn't give me a call to that effect, and I don't remember these details. Had the commander called, I would have written in the entry, Commander's call, do this and that. The entry would state that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we don't want to suggest that Pandurevic is calling you from where he is. Let's say it's Dragan Obrenovic that's calling you. But just as a hypothetical, the person in charge, in command, tells you to get them an excavator. Couldn't you call Birac Holding and arrange to borrow one of their excavators?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I could not have been given the order because I didn't know where the sort of machinery could be obtained from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think that will wrap up that page. Let's go to the next page, 5741 of 377. And we're now at 123. Sorry, we took the book away from you. Hopefully we've opened it at the right page. I'll try not to let that happen again. Now, you're looking at that page where at the top it says, "Take all measures to avoid surprises." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, is all the handwriting on that page yours?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn the page and go next in order. So it's 124. And you'll see in the top of the page it says: "Vukotic and Petkovic."

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, where does your handwriting stop on this page?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the point where another pen is used, below Lovac 1 and Lovac 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then if you could, just for one second, turn the page to 5743, you'll see that your handwriting starts up again, maybe a quarter of the way down the page.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go back to where we were, 5742, that page that begins "Vukotic and Petkovic." Now, these entries of somebody else's hand, whose hand is that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What time of day could that have happened -- did that occur?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It may have been the assistant duty officer who wrote this, but I don't know what time of day it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this could have been the time of day that somebody like Momir Nikolic came by when you weren't around; right?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, isn't it possible that Momir Nikolic came around the time that you were off for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I repeat, I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, how about Colonel Beara? We see him mentioned here. Did you see him around the Zvornik Brigade any time on these days, the 13th, 14th, 15th, 16th?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember meeting Mr. Beara at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you don't remember meeting or seeing Mr. Vujadin Popovic either, do you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't remember him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you don't remember seeing or meeting Drago Nikolic on these days either?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said that that was the case. I didn't see Drago Nikolic either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you didn't see Vinko Pandurevic when he came back on the 15th and went to the headquarters even though you were at the headquarters at the same time; right? You didn't see him either?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That too, I said, that I didn't see him when he came to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about this reference. You would have, of course, reviewed the duty officer notebook when you got back to see what had happened in your absence; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I probably cast a glance. I don't remember. I also don't remember if I took any steps because from what the entry said, I didn't feel that there was any need to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's see what this says. The part I'm interested in is at the bottom of the page and it says: "President of the municipality, Mitrovic, called and asked that the flatbed trailer (Colonel Beara)" and then crossed out, "be sent to Bratunac to bring a bulldozer 1.000. Colonel Beara passed on the message." Can you tell us what that means, "Colonel Beara passed on the message"?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's what the text says. What it means ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, just explain to me what the text says.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can read what the text says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, explain to me what that means.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't make an inference on the basis of what it says. It says that Mr. Stevo Kostic should get in touch with Aco -- or, rather, president of the Mitrovica municipality asked for at a trailer truck to be towed to Bratunac, that bulldozer 1.000 should be sent, received by Colonel Beara --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Conveyed by Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, was this message about the bulldozer conveyed by Colonel Beara or conveyed to Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says conveyed by Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did he convey the message to? Who did Beara convey the message to?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says "President of the Mitrovic municipality called that a trailer truck be sent to Bratunac in order to transport a bulldozer, conveyed by Colonel Beara."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that the same bulldozer -- any relationship to the dozer that you had written about earlier?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you had something called a delivery book, didn't you? I'll show you the original. I don't know if you -- you remember this red book?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not before I look at the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This red book, just looking at it now, doesn't ring any bells at all?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm handing that to you. That's P289. You want to look in it and see if it refreshes your recollection at all? Just -- the front of it has been translated in English for people, it's "Delivery Book Kp-6." You were talking in your testimony earlier that there should be records of deliveries to Orahovac. Wouldn't this book be a possible source of reflecting those records?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it's reflected in this book, but I said that there was documentation, not a book but sheets of delivery which can be found in the bookkeeping records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what is this book?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This book contains records of certain destinations to which transportation was effected -- of bread or rationed food or -- I don't know. At any rate, the authenticity or, rather, the authentic records of everything that was issued from warehouses in terms of food, equipment, and the rest, are the -- are sheets that I referred to, the documents. This is an auxiliary tool used by the logistics sector to record shipments effected at certain periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Shipments of food and other things like you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it says bread, rations, and what else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you before I have a look at this. This is the first time I'm leafing through this book, and it's very difficult for me to tell you what it is that the records refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were the assistant commander for logistics. You've just said that this was a Zvornik Brigade logistics record. There is no mystery to it. You recognise what is going on with this book. Materiels were getting sent out to various places, to various people, bread is going to soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the records reflect what happened on whose behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. This is very simple and we won't spend much time with it. I just want you to go to a particular page. It should be marked there with one of those little yellow sticky things on the side, you see on the side. It's P00289, and B/C/S, 116; English, page 8. And the ERN is 0114-8797.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could blow that up. It's that left top side of the page. We can see that on the top of the page it's handwritten 13 July 1995, Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then as we go down, it has 1600, 1400. And then what is the next time under 1400 Petkovci? What time is that for Orahovac? Sir, can you just read the numbers? You're used to reading those numbers.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think that what it says is 0100 Orahovac, but I can't decipher it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's what I think it says, too. 0100 hours, Orahovac. And then it says "police"; right? It's really short, very simple. It says, "0100 hours Orahovac - police."

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why it is that you're asking me this. At 1.00 on the 13th, I was resting. If you hadn't read out this word "police," I would not have been able to decipher it. But now that you told me, I can confirm yes, it says "police."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, well, perhaps this refreshes your recollection. On the evening hours of 13 July, several bus loads of Muslim prisoners came to the Orahovac school. We have a Muslim that survived the execution that has told us that, and there has been one, two, I think two MPs from the Zvornik Brigade that say that they were there that night. And if there is Zvornik MPs at the school in Orahovac that night, this is a -- this is a record of them being taken some sort of supplies; isn't it? You're the duty officer. You're the logistics guy. This is duty officer, logistics, Orahovac, it's all coming together for you.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know of any events in Orahovac until my arrival there in the afternoon hours of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another document, P00290. And I will give you a photocopy of this. I think I've got the original, but I think the photocopy will work. Now, this is another one of these documents we dug up out of the Zvornik Brigade collection, and we'll give you the original just so you can check the signature and the stamp. Take your time to take a look at it. What is this?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's the municipality of Zvornik taking fuel in the warehouse of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mean the municipality giving fuel to the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since in certain cases we didn't have enough fuel, it was necessary to engage the services of the municipality to get the required quantities. Sometimes we would not receive sufficient quantities of fuels on request of the Drina Corps, and then we were forced to turn to the municipality to provide fuel necessary for the brigade to be operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 223 in the B/C/S, sorry. Sorry, if we could just get the number sorted out. We're almost done with the last exhibit or two. We'll just get that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Take your time and look at it. Page 223. That's the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No it's not. Sorry, 222. We're almost there. That's it. If we could have the English up as well -- sorry. Let me put the English, I apologise, somehow we missed in English. If we could get that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this, sir? We can see under the remarks, can you read the remarks slowly so we can try to translate it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the delivery sheet relating to the receipt of items which records the receipt of fuel at the petrol pump in Karakaj, and the fuel arrived -- or, rather, was supplied by Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. Can you read what's in the middle of the page, it starts with "Remark ..."

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says 1.748 litres of D2 were put into the petrol pump tank. 200 litres were given for the motor vehicle, registration plate number ZV 33426, that is transporting -- and 52 litres water extraction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not sure what this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. On the 13th and the 14th and the 15th and the 16th of July, there were a lot of vehicles taking thousands of Muslims from schools to execution sites, buses, TAM trucks, where did the fuel come from for that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to what was found out later, the fuel for these purposes was provided by the corps. Now I remember this document and that fuel was received from the municipality. Because the situation with the fuel in the Zvornik Brigade was, on many occasions, at the minimum level and quite often we didn't have enough supplies for our regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How, do you know the fuel for the operation to execute the Muslims prisoners was provided by the corps?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that they provided fuel for execution. I only said that in emergency situations requests were made to the corps to provide fuel, but there was no was no request from our brigade of that nature forwarded either to the municipality or to the corps, as far as I know and as far as I can remember. So for these specific purposes, there was no request sent by the Zvornik Brigade to any quarters for these specific purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you said as far as you can remember, so you might have forgot?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, one can check that from the documents, whether there are any request existed and for what purposes the request was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P00291.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document you have seen before. I think you and I went over it. I'll give you a hard copy to -- well, I'll give you an original. Take a look at this. We've talked about this before; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a few questions. We see it's in the left-hand dated the 16th of July, and under the name and the address of recipient it says KDK, that should be command Drina Corps, I think, not commander. The addressee station for Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you knew what Popovic's job -- Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic's job was in July of 1995, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic's job was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I know that he was with the corps security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what I'm interested in is as we go down we see that this is diesel fuel, D2. And it says: "PG is issued according to the order of Captain S. Milosevic. Out of 500 litres of D2, 140 litres were returned." And then we see a signature of somebody. So this says you issued an order. Tell us about that order.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I already told you that this is an incorrect document as far as I can see. It is impossible to use the same sheet in order to receive and issue fuel. That is incorrect procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we are not really concerned about whether it's incorrect or not, but that's -- I appreciate that, I can tell you that according to -- this fuel got where it was going to. So tell us about the order you issued. And I'm just reading what it says, what order did you issue?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to read what is written here, and it says here that fuel should be issued to the Drina Corps command that will be taken over by Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic at the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. We see that. But go down further. Go down to the handwritten remarks where it starts talking about diesel fuel. We can all see it in the original language. It says you issued a -- you issued the order.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that it was possible for me to issue this kind of order since I signed this on the 17th of July, not on the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, the fuel we know went out on the 16th, and this document says it went out under your order. Now, Captain, I am not thinking you're the guy that's running the show here, but who did you get your order from. When you are dispensing fuel, who do you normally get your order from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have a reference where this guy said that it was dispatched under the order of this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm reading the English translation, "PG," which stands for fuel, "is issued according to the order of Captain S. Milosevic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but okay -- I can see it in English. All right. You should be able to see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was said that some guy said it, as far as I see the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean is you can see it on the monitor now. It's the third line in the body of the document. There. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, sir, I am not saying that you were the originator of this business. Who did you receive your order to dispense this fuel? Who gave you your order?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember who gave this order. All I know is that we didn't have enough fuel. I mentioned that several times. And therefore this shows that we issued this fuel and that a certain amount of the fuel had to be returned to the brigade. I can only assume that it came from the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Whose signature is that that we see there right under the word -- well, it looks like it's right under the number 500?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recognise this signature under the number 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So tell us what you remember about this order and this fuel?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, the Zvornik Brigade had only its fuel levels at the minimum, and then came an order from the corps command for us to -- actually, for the fuel to be issued to us and that we shall be recompensed for this fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the fuel went to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, it wasn't clear to me where Mr. Popovic was. I just saw his name there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But this fuel, according to this document, went to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't deny that, that it went to Popovic, but I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, how much more time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ten or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My suggestion is that with the okay of those who are working harder than we are, we continue and finish soon after the cross-examination unless there are further questions -- yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have quite a bit of a re-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Really? We will come tomorrow as well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I am sure you remember all the fuel that was needed to bury those thousands of people up in the Branjevo-Pilica area on the 17th of July, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about these activities. I know that Muslims were executed, but I don't know anything about the needs or the supplies of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you know Popovic was in the area of Zvornik at the time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had no idea about Pilica, I take it, that its fuel went to Pilica?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P0041.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'll give you a version of that as well. Sir, what happened to those thousands of Muslims that were buried near the schools in the Zvornik area? Did they get dug up and moved?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I heard stories that bodies were moved from one location to another, but I don't know where they were moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a 15 minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we had left off you were looking at the document dated 14 September, and I was asking about what you knew about the reburial of thousands of Muslim men. What's this -- we see this in this document P0041 that it provides 5 tonnes of diesel fuel. It's from the logistic sector of the Main Staff to the Standard Barracks to Captain Milorad Trpic, but that's got to be Milorad Trbic; right?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I would like to emphasise once again that I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that should be Milorad Trbic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says Captain Milorad Trpic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, surely if 5 tonnes of diesel came into the unit, you as assistant commander for logistics would know about it; right?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. Quite simply, I know nothing about this amount of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it a question of memory, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot change my memory. I cannot refresh my memory. What I cannot remember, I cannot remember, and I say again I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, this document would have gone to the logistics sector, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's specified here who the recipient is in the Zvornik Brigade, but I would like to underline that I -- it didn't reach my desk. I never received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should have gone to the logistics sector, though, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says, "To the command," it doesn't say to the logistics sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, it's a simple question. This document related to fuel should have gone to the logistic sector, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I'm telling you that I didn't receive this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll try again, sir. Should a copy of this document have gone to the logistics sector?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not receive this letter. This doesn't deal with the fuel required by the Zvornik Brigade. Had that been the case, then it would be specified like that and in that case it would reach the logistics sector. And Captain Trbic would not be in charge of this fuel but rather Captain Milosevic if it was intended for the logistics support of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, who is your chief that deals with fuel?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The chief of traffic service was Mr. Pantic. The chief of technical service was Mr. Krstic. The usual procedure, when it comes to fuel and issue of fuel for the needs of battalions, the person in charge was Mr. Pantic. And in principle it was within the purview of the technical service, meaning that they were responsible for fuel. Why was that the case? The reason was because for one period of time we didn't have the chief of the technical service, and Mr. Krstic, when he came to take this position, he needed some time to learn about the job, and I'm not sure whether he managed to do that because Mr. Krstic was a civilian, and he was an engineer by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Pantic was your fuel guy. Pantic should have seen this document; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whether he should have seen that or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's put the original full up on the screen, and I want you to look up in the right-hand corner of this document. What's that word, up in the right-hand corner, that's handwritten in?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it reads "Pantic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this went to Pantic; right?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. As I said, I am not familiar with this document. I was not informed about Pantic receiving this document. Therefore, I cannot confirm any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to P00379.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The last little bit on this topic. And we are going to the duty officer notebook of 14 September. It's B/C/S 115, English 115. And I'll show you the original. So if you look down, sir, you'll see here in the duty officer book, and I can tell you that this is -- these are the numbers down here that have to do with this document we just looked at and another one just like it, both of which have Pantic written in the corner. And here it actual says "delivered to Pantic." So you can confirm for us now that according to these records this fuel -- or, excuse me, these documents related to the fuel went to Pantic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you can assist me, I can't find the sentence that you have just read. On which page is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's down at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you see that little star, look upon the --

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you see where I'm referring you to now?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I really apologise. I can't see the name "Pantic" on this page. If you can help me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's on the left-hand side where the little yellow marker is that I gave to you, right by your left-hand.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well -- there you go. That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's written in the Cyrillic script, and I'm going to try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on that word, please. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He should look at the display. He looks at the book, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But don't you think this is even better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the asterisk, where you pointed me to, it says: Telegram, strictly confidential, 03/4, and then date 14th of September, 1995. And then again another telegram, the 14th of September, and it says "to Pantic," as far as I can make it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thanks for clarifying that. So if -- and I can tell you that the fuel document you were looking at before is one of those two numbers. So this would mean that this actually -- this document went to Pantic, so Pantic would have been fully aware of this fuel; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the entry into the duty officers' book, and it is up to Pantic to confirm whether he received the telegram or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you're his superior. He reports to you. You would know what he knew on something like this coming from General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he didn't notify me of this. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see. All right. Let me ask you another question. We looked through the duty officer notebook, and we looked for any time anyone at the front gate would have called up the duty officer to tell them that a soldier or an officer was at the front gate. And I looked through that whole book -- well, I've looked through it, my colleague behind me read it, and there were no references in that book of any military man being called to the attention of the duty officer. There was one reference where a civilian came by looking for Legenda.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about it. I would have entered the information if anybody showed up. I was a duty officer during my service in Bijeljina, and my instructions were that should anyone show up, the front gate should place a call, the person should be escorted to where he wants to go, and an entry should be made in the log-book. That is how I understood the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But that's not how it practically worked out, is it? We know that from the book.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about it. I emphasise that I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you testified. Mr. Bourgon was asking you questions. You clearly said that it gets written in the book, it would have been in the book if it happened. You want to withdraw that testimony now?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not want to withdraw it. I stand by my position. I am convinced that this is the way that this work should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You remember testifying in the state court?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've got an English version of this. And you were asked a question on page 19, I'll read it slowly. It's about the time you were at Orahovac: "But when you arrived there nearby the school, were the trucks already is there?" That's the question by the Prosecutor. You say: "I don't remember exactly if they were already there, but upon my arrival, the time I was there, I think -- I think I can go back a little. There already was a vehicle that was prepared, and I don't know the exact time when I arrived and when -- when they started driving people off, I other words. When I got there, I noticed a vehicle here, and they were already loading people on that vehicle." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I said. And that's what I observed when I got there. I repeated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you knew then and there that those people were going to be killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it goes on. We'll go down to the bottom of the page of page 20 in English, and the Prosecutor says: "So they had a blindfold and they were loaded on to trucks. Who made all these necessary preparations?" And you say: "I don't know who made the preparations, only when I got there and saw this case and heard this case, then I felt that I'd been cheated, that I hadn't come to secure prisoners in a building. And I requested to be allowed to leave. I entered a nearby house where they offered us some coffee, and from there, I requested there a telephone -- a civilian telephone in the house. I asked for a duty operations officer to send me a vehicle so I could go back to the brigade." I'll take up to the -- and I'll repeat it, so it's very clear to you. It says here: "I hadn't come to secure prisoners in a building, and I requested to be allowed to leave." Who did you request to be allowed to leave from?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that I put it quite that way, that I was seeking permission. There was nobody to seek permission from. I said that once I saw what was going on there, I felt that I was tricked, and I wanted to find a way to go back to the brigade and be gone from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're saying this is wrong?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I described what happened in the same words that I described it now, that I had nobody to ask permission from. I simply asked for a way to be found for me to be transported back to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask the Trial Chamber to let me -- to put the witness just two questions, all of them related to the fuel and document which the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- asked in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Milosevic. Let me introduce myself to you although you know me. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and I am counsel for Vujadin Popovic in this case. Let us look at document 291, 291 that the Prosecutor showed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the bottom part of the document shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The column -- or, rather, the row showing signatures. Can you tell me if you can see from this document that Vujadin Popovic in fact received fuel?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we first look at the top of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the document that the Prosecutor showed you in relation to 500 litres of fuel and 140 which were returned?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't conclude on the basis of the document that Popovic received it. Can we go back to the signature block? It says "received by Branko Bogdanovic," or, rather, sorry, Branko Bogicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall ever seeing a document which would indicate that Popovic had received the fuel?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive information, and I'm excluding Prosecution here from anyone else, to the effect that Popovic had received this shipment of fuel?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon, we have to finish by not later than quarter to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will do my best to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise we will have to come -- or, rather, you will have to come again tomorrow because we are here every day in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If it was just for me, Mr. President, no problem, but I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am sure you will do your best.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... for the others in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am sure you will do your best.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Milosevic. I have a few questions for you. At page 42, line 23 today, my colleague suggested to you that you did not issue any orders in Orahovac and you confirmed that. What I would like to know is in your portion, as assistant commander for logistics, how often did you issue orders to other soldiers of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't issue any orders to other units in the brigade. My orders were intended only for my chiefs of logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have P406 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I refer to page 45, line 16 where you were asked questions about this document. I'm sorry, this is not the wrong -- it's the wrong document. I am talking about the document which talked about uniforms. Oh, 4600, I apologise. Sir, this is a document that was shown to you by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm whether this document talks about uniforms being received by the Zvornik Brigade on 17 July?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then we'll be here tomorrow morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, what does this document say?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says sewing and embroidery workshop and receipt of military post. This document doesn't indicate that it was received by anyone in a unit. If you scroll down, you will see that nobody signed on behalf of the brigade as having received the batch of uniforms and as having stored the uniforms in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Does this document include any information about uniforms being issued by the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Does this document contain any information that the uniforms which are indicated there are new uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The document indicates that the uniforms are camouflage uniforms. Now, whether they are new or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Does that change anything in this document to your testimony that in July 1995 you might have had some used documents but not new uniforms -- sorry, old uniforms but not new uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said that we used the existing uniforms, the M77 uniforms. This is the first time I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on page 45, line 1, my colleague asked you questions about Pantic sending ammunition to Rocevic. He did not ask you the specific questions, whether you were aware of that. So I am just asking, were your aware that ammunition had been sent to Rocevic by Pantic on 15 July?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As assistant commander for logistics, how much are you aware of the daily activities of your section chiefs, what they do from minute to minute every day? How much of this are you aware?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was able to know from my meetings following the briefings with the commander, I would convey orders which I received at the briefing to provide security of the various battalions. I did not interact with them frequently, and from this document I can see that there were matters I was not privy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have P4602 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that was also used by my colleague. Can you confirm if by this document you are issuing or requesting equipment?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I've seen the document for the first time here. I did say that I signed it. With this document, I asked that the Zvornik Brigade be -- that its request be met, but on the basis of the document you can't really say if it was received by the brigade, and I don't recall if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who was this equipment being requested from? Who are you asking to give you equipment?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The request was sent to the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is there anything in this document that says that you are asking this equipment for Srebrenica purposes?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nowhere in the document does it state that the request was made for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving any specific order asking you to provide any equipment specifically for the purposes of the troops going to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall a document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: P377. And I would like to refer you to page ending in 5737. If the original can be given to the witness, maybe we can go a bit quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to know if on this page, 5737, if there is any of your writing on this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You might want to direct him to the ERN and make sure he's looking at the right --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, ERN number, I believe it would be at the bottom or at the top. 5737 would be the last four digits for that page. Maybe we can have it also in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, the page is in e-court now, sir, before you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The first two sentences seem to be written on my hand. It says, Sreco, they should prepare their platoons, and he should be ready to leave within half an hour if he calls in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the rest of the document, the rest of this page, is there any of your writing?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I move to the next page, ERN 5738, you've already confirmed to my colleague that this is all your writing except the last line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The last three lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Last three lines. Now, is that the first -- looking at the -- your writing on this page, is that when you took over your duty on 13 July? Can you say this?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think so. It says the 13th of July in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the middle of the page it says at some point 0950. Based on these numbers, at -- the last three lines which are not in your writing would have been written, at the minimum, at what time, at the earliest?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can conclude that it must have been after 9.50, because in the upper right-hand corner, it says "9.50, call all logistics battalions," and then no entry for time was made below. I can't remember when it could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you can turn to page -- to 5739, are there any time entries on this page?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No time entries were made on this page either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the next page, what is the first time entry?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So on this basis, what is the latest that those three lines not in your writing could have been written?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The entries that were made by someone else and not by me is at -- on the page 3542 from the middle to the bottom, and on the following page the first paragraph was not written by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my question wasn't precise. Go back to the three lines which are not in your writing on page 5738. You see those three lines, the last three lines of 5738?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: All right. If you go back to the page I was referring to where you mention the first time entry as being 1315, what do you conclude that -- when were these lines written at the latest?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't say. I can only say that it was between 9.50 and 1315.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned today at page 21, line 12, that you went to bed at midnight on the 13th of July. Do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, do you recall whether before you went to bed your assistant made any entries in the book?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you go to page 5742. If your assistant did not make any writing while you are there, then what is the earliest time these entries there can have been entered?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They could have been made between 2400 hours and 5.00 in the morning on the night between the 13th and the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you move to the next page, when your writing changes again, which is 5743, at what time did this -- did you take-over your duty?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The time when I took the duty shift over from the assistant is not stated here, but I do know that it's normally at 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you go back to page 5742 at the bottom, you were asked a few questions about this. The last three lines, you confirm to my colleague that this is not your writing. Were you told about this information at any time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that I was at any time. I don't remember the information at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you told at any time when you resume your duty in the morning of 14th July whether Beara had called during the night?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I resumed my duty on the morning of the 14th, at 5.00, when I took over from my assistant, I was not told any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I go to page 5740, questions were put to you by my colleague concerning the bulldozer or the dozer in your writing. Had you received a request by anybody to find a dozer, how would you do it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that I received a request to that effect. I suppose that such a request would not have been addressed to me. Being a technical matter, it would have been sort of somebody who deals with that sort of machinery, i.e., the engineers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have P289 in e-court. And this will be my last series of questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, this was the book that was shown to you concerning certain equipment being shipped, I think. I would like to go to the same page which the Prosecution was using, and that -- the exact page number was 116 in B/C/S and page 8 in English. Now, the information looking at what you -- and the Prosecution agreed that this was at 0100 in the morning. Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I went to sleep at 1200 hours on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you informed about anything being shipped to Orahovac at 1.00 in the morning? Were you informed of that at any time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you tell from this entry what was shipped to Orahovac at 1.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Have you seen this book before?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are there other documents that record shipments made and materiel issued?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said on several occasions that there existed delivery sheets which would be filled out against the materiel issued from the warehouse for the purposes of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if you go down this page where it says 14 July, 1995, do you see any indication of anything being shipped to Orahovac on 14 July?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Based on this document, does that change your testimony of what you said today, that you did not order and you did not see any food arriving in Orahovac on 14 July?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do not change my testimony. I didn't see it, and I didn't know about any sort of food arriving in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, today on page 74, the Prosecution put a question to you concerning that there were no entries in the duty book about a military policeman that called. My question was the following: What would you write in the book, that a military policeman called you from the gate, or would you write the names and the particulars of the person visiting? Which information would you enter in the book?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As can be seen from my entries in the book, I wrote everything; who appeared, the calls that were made, and if I was on duty that day, I would write everything. I would say that somebody who belonged to another brigade had come to visit the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Looking at the -- I think you still have P377 before you -- nope, P -- that's the duty book, I think you have this in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have this in e-court. And I'd like to go to page 5750.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you have this page, sir, 5750?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The last line on this page, can you say what it says?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "CJB - Lanej [phoen], 100-troop-strong unit is arriving."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you're not on duty that day, but what does that this appear to say, or what's your understanding of those lines written by the duty officer on that day?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that the operations duties officer was called and an entry was made about this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What would you have been written in the book on 13 July if a unit of 100 soldiers had arrived?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose I would note down the source of the call, if it was a CJB, and if the person -- if the caller introduced themselves, I would write down their name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we leave it here, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I am done, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milosevic. I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Mr. Milosevic, we are finished with your testimony. You will be ushered out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I only have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- one document which was the one that was marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it would be IC3D110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections from anyone? That's the plan of the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. Yes. No objections, so admitted. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, the list has gone around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have five documents. Any objections? I hear none. So these five documents are also admitted. The only thing that I notice is that the first one has an MFI behind the number. Is that because it's still MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was MFI'd by the Popovic team. We're not sure why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's that huge red book -- or the big red book, and we just wanted that one page about the 13th and the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Anything that is not yet translated will remain MFI'd until it is. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just one thing, it's not a document, but during the course of his cross-examination, Mr. McCloskey took the witness through the duty officers' notebook for the 13th of July, and on page 123 of Exhibit P377 in the middle of the page appears, in a box, Vinko and two phone numbers. We're all agreed that is no reference to my client at all, and I spoke to Mr. McCloskey about this, and I thought it appropriate to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree to that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I think on the record somewhere it's who that is, but that's my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I saw you standing up, Mr. Bourgon. But you have second thoughts. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 6.55 p.m. sine die.
